job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Karl Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at seven in a flat in Partick that I share with an old school friend, and I walk to a mid-size accounting firm near Buchanan Street. I'm a trainee on the tax compliance team, so I prepare returns for small companies and a few sole traders, and a senior reviews them. Two evenings a week I study for my professional exams, and on Saturdays I play football for a pub team.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get that job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did a finance degree and finished with a good result, and I had one internship at a bank's back office. Then I applied to twelve firms and got two offers. My uncle Emeka is an accountant in London, and he's the one who told me to take the firm that pays for the exams. My mum runs a hair salon and my dad drives a bus, so they can help if I'm stuck, but I owe about 15 thousand in loans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's a useful tool, like spreadsheets were. I'd tell friends not to panic and not to cheer, because every new technology gets sold as magic and then settles down. Online I'd stay out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my career runs as planned. I'd qualify in three years and move to a manager role by about 27. My money is tight with the loans, but my job feels secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying and use the firm's software for the easy parts of returns. I'd put 200 a month in savings and try to reach a six-month cushion. I'd also start an index fund with 50 a month, since the market's long-term and I'm young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like predictable, and this is a predictable world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your job feels secure. Is there anything that could change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm could lose a big client or a partner might retire and sell up. That's the real risk in a mid-size firm, more than technology. If it happened I'd have the exam credit and a decent reputation, so I'd get another place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're paying 15 thousand in loans. How does that sit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, honestly. It comes out of my pay in small amounts and I treat it like a bill. I'd rather build a cushion than race to clear it.

say: I'd say it's a **useful tool**, like spreadsheets were, and a good help with returns.
I'd tell friends not to **panic** or cheer, because every new technology settles down.
think: My career runs as planned: **qualify** in three years, manager by about 27.
My job feels secure even though the **loans** keep money tight.
do: Keep studying for the **professional exams** and use the firm's software.
Save **200 a month** towards six months of cover.
Start an **index fund** with 50 a month.
feel: **Calm**, because I like predictable and this world is predictable.
S0.quote: Every new technology gets sold as magic and then settles down.
fieldNote: Karl's calm comes from a **funded qualification** and a steady firm.
He names real risks, such as the firm losing a client, with no drama.
His centre outlook shows in distrust of confident predictions.

steps.text: Study for the professional tax exams two evenings a week
Keep preparing tax returns for small companies at the firm
Save 200 a month towards a six-month cushion
Start a 50 a month index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's see what actually works and keep a human check on it. I'd test the tools on a few returns and report back. Online I'd share the sensible articles and ignore the loud ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried. Tax compliance is a lot of the work the card names: checking, planning and answering questions. The firm will probably want fewer juniors, and more review by seniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the firm's new tools as soon as they roll out, and learn what they get wrong, since that's the bit a reviewer needs. I'd shift toward advisory work, talking to clients about their situation. I'd also stay on the exam track and save 250 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. I can see what the next two years might look like, and I have a few options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn what the tools get wrong. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By running a return both ways, by hand and with the tool, then comparing. I ran a return both ways, by hand and with the new software, and found the software missed a small-business allowance. I told the senior and she thanked me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you think the firm is taking you seriously?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they kept hiring trainees and told us the plan. If they quietly stopped, I'd start applying elsewhere within a month.

say: I'd say let's see what **actually works** and keep a human check.
I'd test the tools on a few returns and **report back**.
think: Tax compliance is mostly the **checking** work the card names.
The firm will want fewer **juniors** and more review by seniors.
do: Use the firm's new **tools** and learn where they go wrong.
Move toward **advisory** work, talking to clients.
Stay on the exam track and save **250 a month**.
feel: **Anxious**, but not frozen, as there are a few options.
S1.quote: I ran a return both ways, by hand and with the new software, and found the software missed a small-business allowance.
fieldNote: Karl tests tools **empirically**, which suits his steady, evidence-led profile.
He sets a clear tripwire: hiring stops, he starts applying elsewhere.
His anxiety is about the junior layer, not about being unemployable.

steps.text: Run returns by hand and with the tool, and note the differences
Ask to join the client advisory team within the year
Keep passing the professional exam papers on schedule
Save 250 a month into a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd ask the partners straight out what the plan is, and I'd say we need clarity within a month. Online I'd say two years is a very short window and that we need governments to act.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the trainee role as it exists is done. The exams take three years, and the thing they qualify me for may not exist by then. I'd have a bit of time, maybe a year, but I wouldn't count on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save as much as I could, about 500 a month, and cut anything that isn't rent or food. I'd ask the firm if I could move to client-facing work now, while they still have a use for me. And I'd talk to my uncle Emeka about whether any kind of finance work holds up, and I'd look at hands-on options as a plan B.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a bit numb. I'd have the sensation of being in a queue that's moving faster than I can think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said hands-on options as plan B. What would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad knows people in the bus depot, and there's maintenance and dispatch. It wouldn't be glamorous, but it's work. I'd rather have a plan B that exists than a plan A that doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your friend who shares the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we should both save the rent for three months in an account we don't touch. He works in marketing, so he's in the same boat, and it would be silly to panic separately.

say: I'd ask the partners what the **plan** is and give them a month.
I'd say **two years** is a very short window.
think: The trainee role as it exists is **done**, and exams take three years.
I'd have maybe **a year**, but I wouldn't count on it.
do: Save about **500 a month** and cut everything but rent and food.
Ask the firm for **client-facing** work while they still have a use for me.
Ask my uncle **Emeka** which finance jobs hold up, and keep bus depot work as plan B.
feel: **Anxious** and a bit numb, as if in a queue moving faster than I can think.
S2.quote: I'd rather have a plan B that exists than a plan A that doesn't.
fieldNote: Karl's reaction is a **practical plan**, with named fallback jobs through his dad.
He worries about the exam timeline mismatching the machine timeline.
Suggests his friend save jointly, a social, not isolated, response.

steps.text: Save about 500 a month and cut everything except rent and food
Cut the pub football subs and nights out
Ask the firm to move me to client-facing work now
Call uncle Emeka and ask my dad about bus depot maintenance jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is enough to finish exams, if we're sensible. I'd tell colleagues to learn the tools now and not wait for the firm. Online I'd say that people should plan rather than argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine if I got qualified and moved quickly into advisory work. Five years is tight, but I'd be a qualified accountant by year three, and that might hold some value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the exams steadily and aim to move to a client team, then a niche, like small-business advice. I'd save 400 a month and keep 20 percent as cash. I'd also try one side project, helping a few sole traders with their books, since two have asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. It feels like a long run-up with a hard stop at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the qualification might hold some value. What if it doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have wasted three years, but I'd still have the knowledge. I'd rather know the rules and not need them than need them and not know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Emeka, my uncle, and my friend Callum from uni who is in audit in Manchester. We'd compare notes every few months. Two cheap opinions are better than one.

I'd tell colleagues to learn the **tools** now and not wait.
think: I'd be fine if I qualified and moved quickly into **advisory** work.
Five years is tight, but a qualified **accountant** by year three might hold value.
do: Take the exams **steadily** and move to a client team, then a niche.
Save **400 a month** and keep 20 percent as cash.
Help a few sole traders with their **books** on the side.
feel: **Uneasy**, not scared, like a long run-up with a hard stop.
S3.quote: I'd rather know the rules and not need them than need them and not know.
fieldNote: Karl treats five years as a **window for qualifying**, then specialising.
He values cheap second opinions: his uncle Emeka and a university friend.
Side work for sole traders is a concrete step, not a fantasy.

steps.text: Pass the next two exam sittings and finish within three years
Move to a client team, then small-business advice
Save 400 a month and keep 20 percent as cash
Do books for two sole traders on weekends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and the sensible thing is to keep learning and keep options open. At work I'd carry on as normal. Online I'd stay quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fairly calm. By 2036 I'd be 32, with a qualification, savings and maybe a mortgage. Ten years gives me time to change direction twice if I need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, build my client base, and get a decent deposit in about six years. I'd save about 300 a month and put some in the index fund. I'd also keep one new skill going at all times, whether it's data or advisory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, though I'd not stop watching. It feels like a normal career with a big question mark at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd change direction twice. What would those be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably from compliance to advisory, then maybe to running a small practice or a role in a company. I wouldn't plan the second yet, because I'd want to see what the machine does first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make this world less safe than it feels?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the first five years went as slowly as a plateau and then everything came at once. Ten years can be a trap if I coast through the first half.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time**, so keep options open.
At work I'd carry on as **normal**.
think: I'd be fairly calm, since I'd be **32** with qualifications and maybe a mortgage.
Ten years gives me time to **change direction** twice.
do: Qualify, build a **client base** and aim for a deposit in about six years.
Save **300 a month** and put part in the index fund.
Keep one new **skill** going at all times.
feel: **Calm**, with a big question mark at the end of a normal career.
S4.quote: Ten years can be a trap if I coast through the first half.
fieldNote: Karl's calm is **conditional on not coasting**, which he names himself.
He plans two direction changes but won't fix the second.
Typical of a steady, pragmatic centre profile.

steps.text: Qualify and build a client base at the firm
Save 300 a month towards a house deposit
Put part of the savings in an index fund each month
Pick up one new data or advisory skill every year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because the exams take three years and the machine wouldn't wait for me to finish. What would help is a clear message from the firm about which jobs stay, and some kind of support while I switch. Honestly I'd also like the exam bodies to say what's still worth studying.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I trust what people say about all this. Everybody on both sides sounds sure, but nobody has done it before. I'd rather prepare for a few possibilities than bet on one.

headlineQuote: Everybody on both sides sounds sure, but nobody has done it before. I'd rather prepare for a few possibilities than bet on one.
portrait: Karl, 22, is a **tax trainee** at a mid-size Glasgow accounting firm, studying for professional exams.
He shares a flat, owes about **15 thousand** and has family who can help in a pinch.
Centre and steady, he tests tools by running **returns** both ways and distrusts confident predictions.
His mood moves from calm to **alarmed** at two years, then back to calm, mainly through a clear plan B.
His uncle Emeka, his friend Callum and his bus-driver dad are his sounding boards.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because the three-year exam path would not finish before the machine arrives.
whatWouldHelp: A clear message from the firm about which jobs stay, and support **while switching**.
